label: Person
name: Abbot Oliba
summary:
Abbot Oliba (c. 971–1046), born Guillem Oliba, was a Catalan nobleman, monk, and bishop who was one of the most significant ecclesiastical and cultural figures of eleventh-century Iberia. Son of Count Oliba I of Berga and Ripoll, he renounced his comital inheritance to become a Benedictine monk at the Abbey of Santa Maria de Ripoll, eventually becoming its abbot (1008) and abbot of Sant Miquel de Cuixà before being consecrated Bishop of Vic in 1018.

Oliba was the principal patron of Romanesque architecture in Catalonia and the western Mediterranean. He commissioned the rebuilding of Ripoll in the grandest Romanesque style — its portal became one of the masterpieces of Romanesque sculpture — and constructed churches at Cuixà, Vic, and elsewhere. His building programme helped establish Romanesque as the dominant architectural vocabulary of Christian Europe.

He was also a pioneer of the Peace and Truce of God movement, convening assemblies in Catalonia that attempted to limit the violence of feudal warfare by establishing protected times (the Truce of God, forbidding fighting from Thursday to Sunday) and protected persons (clergy, merchants, peasants). This movement spread across France and became one of the first attempts at international humanitarian law in the Middle Ages. His intellectual and diplomatic engagement with Rome, Burgundy, and the Catalan counties made him a figure of European stature.
